newsitem.title: USA: ShopKo sees new strategy soon.
newsitem.headline: ShopKo sees new strategy soon.

text.p: - Retailer ShopKo Inc. said Thursday it hopes to set a new corporate plan in the next few weeks following the collapse of its $1 billion merger agreement with Phar-Mor Inc.

The Green Bay, Wis.-based retailer also reported net income rose about 15 percent in its fiscal fourth quarter ended Feb. 22 to $24.3 million, or 76 cents per share, from nearly $21.1 million, or 66 cents a share in the same period a year ago.
The company cited strong performances in its retail and ProVantage health care operations.

"We have the resources and talent to continue building on this strong platform, and intend to explore a variety of options to expand the size and scope of our business," Chief Executive Officer Dale Kramer said in a news release.
In a telephone conference call with investors, Kramer said, "It's a matter of weeks. We have done a lot of the preliminary work previously," he said.
Company executives also hinted the new plan would likely focus on the general merchandise sector rather than the drugstore business as proposed in the now-defunct Phar-Mor deal.
"We believe that we have clearly demonstrated that this concept we currently have developed clearly works, and our preference at this point would be to find similar businesses," Kramer said.
ShopKo and Youngstown, Ohio-based Phar-Mor jointly called off the deal Wednesday, saying it would not have been completed as originally structured.
Sources familiar with the companies cited a decline in Phar-Mor's stock price, regulatory delays and uncertainty about the position of one large Phar-Mor shareholder.
Wall Street had disliked the Phar-Mor deal from the beginning, contending the companies were dissimilar and could not achieve sizable cost-savings. Phar-Mor is a drugstore chain.

ShopKo also said it would take a one-time charge of about $1.6 million to $2 million in after-tax earnings during the first quarter of fiscal 1998 to cover costs associated with the deal's termination.
ShopKo management now will revisit a strategic plan that was developed last spring by financial adviser Salomon Brothers before the Phar-Mor deal was announced.
"We've had no contact with other companies at this point. We'll continue to re-run the (computer) models we ran last spring and take a look at where the opportunities are," Kramer said.

ShopKo officials stressed that one of their major goals is to provide an exit stategy for major shareholder Supervalu Inc. which has announced its intent to divest its position. Supervalu bought ShopKo in 1971 and then sold 54 percent of its stock in a 1991 public offering.
"I think we have a lot of options. The key will be creating the right exit strategy for Supervalu and leaving ourselves in a position where we could make some strategic acquisitions," Kramer said.
ShopKo stock rose 50 cents to $17, and Supervalu edged up 12.5 cents to $29.50 in consolidated afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange. Phar-Mor fell 25 cents to $5.125 on Nasdaq.

ShopKo also said in the conference call that it sees acquisition opportunities to build on its growing ProVantage business. It projected fiscal 1998 sales of ProVantage will rise to $525 million from $349 million in fiscal 1997.
